name: Siddha Natheswarar Temple, Tirunaraiyur (Nachiyar Koil)
deity: Shiva as Siddha Natheswarar (Siddhanatheswarar), with the goddess Soundara Nayaki (Azhagambikai)
period: Tevaram era (hymned 7th century); later Chola structural temple
summary: Tirunaraiyur, beside the famous Nachiyar Koil near Kumbakonam, honours Shiva as Siddha Natheswarar — the lord of the siddhas — with the goddess Soundara Nayaki. A Paadal Petra Sthalam hymned by Sambandar and Sundarar, its legend joins it to the Vaishnava shrine next door: here the sage Medhavi did penance for the wish that Lakshmi be born as his daughter, the wish granted as the goddess Nachiyar of Nachiyar Koil.

sections.history: Tirunaraiyur, whose historical name is Tirunaraiyur Chittechuram, lies about 8–10 km from Kumbakonam on the road to Tiruvarur, in Thanjavur district, right beside the celebrated Nachiyar Koil (the Divya Desam of Srinivasa Perumal and the goddess Nachiyar), scarcely a kilometre away. It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, hymned by Tirugnana Sambandar and Sundarar. The Shiva and Vishnu shrines of Narayur share a single sthala story, and the stone temple is of the Chola period and later.
sections.architecture: A Dravidian temple of the delta, the shrine enshrines Siddha Natheswarar in the sanctum, with the goddess Soundara Nayaki — also Azhagambikai — in her own shrine, a Nandi and the parivara devatas. The lord's name Siddha Natheswarar, 'lord of the siddhas,' recalls the siddha associations of the place, including the healing of Gorakkar; the oil of the lord's abhishekam is held to cure disease.
sections.legends: The great legend joins Shiva to the Vishnu temple next door. The sage Medhavi did penance here with a rare wish — that Mahalakshmi, consort of Vishnu, be born as his daughter — and Shiva conveyed the wish to Vishnu, so that Lakshmi was born as Vanjulavalli and became the Nachiyar of Nachiyar Koil. A siddha legend tells that Gorakkar, afflicted by a skin disease born of a curse, was cured by applying the oil used in the lord's abhishekam — hence Siddha Natheswarar. The place is also called Narapuram, for one Naran, cursed by Durvasa, who worshipped here.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps Maha Shivaratri in Masi (February–March), Navaratri in Purattasi (September–October) and the Mondays of Karthikai, with Pradosha worship. Pilgrims visiting the Nachiyar Koil Divya Desam very often cross to Siddha Natheswarar, honouring the shared story of Shiva and the birth of the goddess.
sections.experience: At Tirunaraiyur the pilgrim stands where Shaiva and Vaishnava devotion meet. Before Siddha Natheswarar, lord of the siddhas, and Soundara Nayaki, and within walking distance of the Nachiyar Koil, the visitor remembers the sage who wished Lakshmi for a daughter and the healing oil of the siddhas — a shrine whose grace reaches across two great traditions.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tirunaraiyur is about 8–10 km from Kumbakonam on the road to Tiruvarur, right beside the Nachiyar Koil (less than 1 km), in Thanjavur district. Kumbakonam is the nearest major rail head, with frequent buses and taxis to Nachiyar Koil and the temple.
